---
title: "Caveats and Performance"
---

What to know before relying on tether in a pipeline: the limits that come from
the model itself, the ones that come from each backend, and what the commands
cost.

## Limits of the model

**Promotion is per system.** `tether promote` fast-forwards a base branch when
it is unchanged since the fork point, uses the native three-way merge where one
exists (git, lakeFS, Dolt), and otherwise refuses with the system's recipe:
Icechunk and Iceberg cannot merge, Lance cannot move a branch head, Neon cannot
promote a child branch. Landing the dataset commit in jj never merges data by
itself.

**No cross-system atomicity.** A commit records each object's state within a
capture window; point-consistency requires quiesced writers. The Neon
quiescence check helps -- `tether commit` refuses while writers are active
unless `--force` -- but nothing coordinates two systems.

**What `undo` can and cannot do.** `jj undo` / `git reset` move the
manifests, never the stores. `tether undo` covers tether's side from its
[operation log](02-concepts.qmd#the-operation-log): a commit is uncommitted
(pins kept), a `new`'s branches are deleted or re-pointed to their recorded
heads, a `gc`'s branches come back but its released pins do not (`tether
repair` recreates them once a manifest references them again, while the
snapshot still exists), a `promote` is refused with the previous heads printed.
A branch that gained writes is never reset or deleted without `--discard` --
by `undo` or by `new`.

**Pin-then-commit ordering.** Pins are created before the VCS commit; if the
commit never lands, the pins leak until `gc` (which scans VCS history plus the
current workspace). Re-run `tether verify` after merging manifests across
branches.

**Forks are lazy.** `new` records which branch each object *will* get; the
first writable `open` creates it from the pin. Workspaces that only read leave
nothing behind, but that first `open` is a store write (no dry run; preview
with `new --eager --dry-run`) and needs the pin to still exist. Objects with
`--pin record` fork during `new` regardless: with no tag, the branch is the
only thing keeping their snapshot or version from expiring. `--eager` or
`[new] fork = "eager"` restores up-front branches.

**Data history costs storage.** Every pin holds bytes in its system until the
commit that names it is dropped and `gc` releases it. `--pin record` skips the
native ref on any backend and forks from the recorded state instead, at the
price of retention-bound recoverability. `commit`, `new`, `gc`, `promote`,
`import`, `repair`, and `upgrade` all take `--dry-run` (and `--plan FILE` /
`--from-plan FILE`) so store writes can be reviewed before they happen. See
[Reclaiming Storage](05-reclaiming-storage.qmd).

**Secrets** are never stored in manifests -- only credential *references* (an
environment variable or secret name). Each backend reads the real credential
from the environment.

## Per backend

**Neon lineage.** Pins are child branches, so a working branch cannot be
deleted while its pins exist (`gc --prune-bookmarks` plans it as kept and
names the pins), `gc` only drops leaf pins, and `new` onto
a *different* pin forks a sibling rather than resetting a branch with children
(`commit` then `new` reuses the branch, since it already sits at the pin).
Neon cannot merge or promote a child into `main`; run production writes on
the trunk bookmark, where the working ref is `main` itself. `protected` needs
a paid plan; branch quotas vary.

**Neon fingerprint cost.** The LSN moves without user writes, so it is a
volatile (address-only) key: only `next_xid` and the branch count as change.
A snapshot may still wake a suspended compute; a plain `status` does not fingerprint (`--snapshot`, `commit`, and `verify` do).

**Files on unversioned storage** are Observed: detectably but not recoverably
drifted. Bucket or container versioning promotes single objects to
Addressable; prefixes stay Observed (tether does not record per-object version
ids). Object-store credentials come from the environment; `[backends.file]
storage_options` in `tether.toml` passes non-secret options (region, endpoint,
account name) to obstore.

**Iceberg catalog variance.** S3 Tables disables maintenance when user refs
exist; use `--pin record` there (forks then come from the snapshot id, valid
until snapshot expiry).

**Delta has no refs.** Versions are recorded, not pinned; `VACUUM` (7-day
default) and log retention (30 days) bound how long `open -r` works. A
recreated table (new metadata id) verifies as drifted, not re-addressed.

**Lance versions are branch-scoped.** State is `(branch, version)`; an
untouched fork reports its parent's address so no-op commits stay no-ops.
Lance refuses to delete a branch a tag references, so a pinned working branch
outlives its bookmark until `gc` drops the tag (a re-fork picks `name.2`).
`--at N` is version `N` of the locator's branch.

**lakeFS staging.** Uncommitted lakeFS changes are not in any commit; a dirty
branch is reported in `status` and refused at `commit`. Pins are
repository-wide: two objects with different prefixes on one branch describe
the same commit and share a pin.

**DuckLake attachments.** A DuckDB-file metadata catalog can be attached only
once per process, so tether attaches per operation and a `DuckLakeHandle` owns
its attachment: `close()` it (or use it as a context manager) before the next
`status`, and do not hold your own writer connection open in the same process.
Postgres, SQLite, and MySQL catalogs have no such limit. Snapshots are
catalog-wide; `table` only scopes the handle. Put `CREATE SECRET` statements in
`[backends.ducklake] init_sql` rather than credentials in the locator.

**Dolt working sets.** Uncommitted changes on a branch are not in any commit;
a dirty branch is reported and refused at `commit`. The password comes from
`$DOLT_PASSWORD` (configurable via `[backends.dolt] password_env`), never the
manifest. Dirty detection needs a Dolt with the `dirty` column on
`dolt_branches`; older servers report clean.

**git remotes.** With `remote` set, a pin is only a pin once the tag push
succeeds: a failed push fails the `pin` and removes the local tag, and `unpin`
deletes on the remote first.

## Performance

tether is an orchestrator; its cost is the network round-trips it fans out,
not Python.

**Fan-out uses threads, not asyncio.** Every backend SDK tether wraps (obstore,
psycopg, pyiceberg, deltalake, lance, lakefs, duckdb, pymysql, `git`) is
synchronous, the per-object Python work is microseconds, and a thread pool
gives the same wall-clock concurrency without forcing an async protocol on
backend authors. `snapshot`, `verify`, and the fork step of `new` all run
concurrently.

**History walks are batched.** `gc`, `verify --all-history`, `repair
--all-history`, and `upgrade` stream every manifest at every commit through
one `git cat-file --batch` process (jj repositories are git-backed, so the
same plumbing applies), caching trees and blobs by object id and verifying
each distinct `(system, state, pin)` once. On a repository with 200 commits
and 5 objects this is ~20-40 ms end to end versus 6-12 s with one process per
read. History *rewrites* (`upgrade`, `abandon`) only read and transform the
commits that touch the dataset directory; under jj the rest are rebased, under
git the answer is cached per subtree id.

**Fingerprints are metadata-only, except the first local one.** A remote
object is one `HEAD`; a prefix is one paged `LIST`; the etag is the store's
content hash. Local files are sha256-hashed so that timestamps do not count as
change, with the hash cached by `(size, mtime_ns, inode)` under
`.tether/cache/`: the first fingerprint of a tree reads every byte (~1.5-3 GB/s
per core, eight files at a time, so disk-bound on NVMe), every later one is an
`os.scandir` walk (~4-20 us per file) plus the files whose stat changed.

**Content diffs are metadata-only too.** Each backend reads manifests, logs,
or catalog tables -- never data -- so `diff --content` costs about one
fingerprint per changed object (two manifest reads for Icechunk and Lance, one
log walk for Delta, one catalog query for DuckLake, one prolly-tree diff for
Dolt). Two stored file listings diff in pure Python at ~50 ms per 100k paths.
